findings.summary: The mnemonic is shown after the layer list but its letters do not match the layer order shown, and the full layer names are repeated on a separate line, so the same list appears twice.
findings.evidence: "Mnemonic: All People Seem To Need Data Processing" followed by "Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical"
findings.fix: Keep the L7-L1 list and the mnemonic only, and label the mnemonic as top-to-bottom. Drop the repeated name line.

findings.summary: The 'What Layering Does' bullets state three ideas as bare fragments and give no visual of the stacked layers or peer-to-peer communication.
findings.evidence: "Each layer serves the layer above it" / "Each layer talks to the same layer on the peer host"
findings.fix: Add a small two-column stack diagram of Host A and Host B with horizontal peer arrows per layer and vertical service arrows.

findings.summary: FCS is introduced as a term without ever being expanded or explained, and the cheat sheet and quiz rely on it.
findings.evidence: "L2 Data Link | MAC addressing, framing, FCS error detection | one link"
findings.fix: Expand on first use: "FCS (Frame Check Sequence): a checksum trailer the receiver uses to detect corrupted frames."

findings.summary: The L5 bullet holds several ideas with examples that are not clearly L5 protocols, and the L6 bullet packs three separate functions (encoding, encryption, compression) into one line.
findings.evidence: "L6 Presentation: encoding, encryption, compression; TLS, JPEG, ASCII/UTF-8"
findings.fix: Split into one bullet for the job and one for examples, or use a Layer | Job | Examples table like the lower layers.

findings.summary: The encapsulation flow is written as a flat list of stacked words with no arrows, so the order and which header wraps what cannot be followed at a glance. The trailer point is also repeated three times.
findings.evidence: "Data / L7-L5 / + TCP header / segment / + IP header / packet / + Eth header + FCS / frame" and "Only Data Link adds a trailer (FCS)" repeated under "Trailer" and in Interview Point
findings.fix: Draw nested boxes or a left-to-right diagram: Data -> [TCP|Data] segment -> [IP|segment] packet -> [Eth|packet|FCS] frame. State the trailer rule once.

findings.summary: The 'Interview Point' section poses questions with answers inline, which makes the page read like prose Q&A rather than scannable notes. The answers repeat earlier content.
findings.evidence: "Which layer adds a trailer? Data Link only, the FCS."
findings.fix: Replace with a short Q | A table or cut the section, since the earlier tables already cover it.

findings.summary: NAT is used to qualify the IP rule but is never defined or explained.
findings.evidence: "NAT rewrites the IP at the boundary"
findings.fix: Add one line defining NAT, for example: "NAT: a router or firewall translates private source IPs to a public IP at the network edge."

findings.summary: The TCP handshake is a flat list of labels with no direction shown, so the sequence cannot be followed as a diagram. The L6 row also lists only TLS and omits other L6 items used on page 2.
findings.evidence: "SYN / client / SYN-ACK / server / ACK / client"
findings.fix: Render as a sequence diagram with client and server lanes and arrows labelled SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK.

findings.summary: The protocol table places TLS at L6 while the 'Common slips' note and page 2 place TLS at L5-L6 and L6 examples; TLS placement is stated inconsistently.
findings.evidence: "L6 | TLS/SSL (L5-L6, not L7)" vs page 2 "L6 Presentation: ... TLS" vs "TLS sits at L5-L6, not only L7"
findings.fix: Use one phrasing everywhere, for example 'TLS: L5-L6 (not L7)', and keep that in a single place.

findings.summary: The Addresses section crams three separate facts about MAC, IP and NAT into adjacent bare lines without a table or hop diagram.
findings.evidence: "MAC: rewritten at every hop / IP: stays end to end / NAT rewrites the IP at the boundary"
findings.fix: Add a small Host -> Router -> Server strip showing which of MAC and IP change at each hop.

findings.summary: The troubleshooting steps are a flat list of layer then hint with no ordering arrow, and the warning bullets at the end repeat points from page 4 and are not tied to any section.
findings.evidence: "L1 / cable, link light / L2 / ARP/MAC, VLAN ..." and "ping is ICMP at L3, not a TCP test / TLS is not only L7"
findings.fix: Render as a numbered bottom-up flow L1 -> L2 -> L3 -> L4 -> L7 and move the repeated slips into one 'Common slips' note.

findings.summary: The 'Remember' line says only a router splits broadcast domains, which contradicts the chapter's own VLAN caveat.
findings.evidence: "A switch splits collision domains; only a router splits broadcast domains." versus the table row "Switch | 1 per port | 1 (unless VLANs)"
findings.fix: Reword to: "A switch splits collision domains; a router (or VLANs, which need a router or L3 switch to talk to each other) splits broadcast domains."

findings.summary: The closing 'Remember' line says only a router splits broadcast domains, which contradicts the VLAN caveat taught on pages 5 and 6.
findings.evidence: "A switch splits collision domains; only a router splits broadcast domains." vs the table row "Switch | 1 per port | 1 (unless VLANs)"
findings.fix: Reword to: "A switch splits collision domains; a router (or VLANs) splits broadcast domains."

findings.summary: The cheat sheet row L7/6/5 lists firewall and load balancer as devices while the L1 row has hub and repeater, and the page's definition of firewall layer conflicts in scope with page 5 which says L3/L4 stateful up to L7.
findings.evidence: "L7/6/5 | data | — | HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH | firewall, load balancer" and "Firewalls and load balancers work from L4 up to L7"
findings.fix: Keep one phrase for the firewall and load balancer span and either list them only in the L4 row or note 'L4-L7' in both rows consistently.

findings.summary: The quiz answer relies on switch flooding of unknown destination MACs, which no earlier page teaches.
findings.evidence: "Unknown destination MAC: the switch floods it" (page 5 only says "Switch forwards only to the destination port")
findings.fix: Add a line on page 5 saying a switch floods a frame out all other ports when the destination MAC is not yet in the CAM table, and that this is how it learns.

findings.summary: The first answer holds multiple ideas in a block, and the unknown-destination flooding point appears as a stray bullet under a question about hubs and switches.
findings.evidence: "TTL also drops by 1, but it was not one of the three" and "Unknown destination MAC: the switch floods it"
findings.fix: Give each question a short answer line plus a bullet list of reasons, and attach the flooding case as an explicit third sub-case labelled for the switch.

findings.summary: Code example is shown before the idea it illustrates is tied to a one-line takeaway, and the mask bullet states no concrete example.
findings.evidence:
Mask says where the network part ends and the host part begins
python
ip = '192.168.10.37'
findings.fix: Add a one-line idea before the code, e.g. 'Each octet converts to 8 binary bits', then show the snippet and its output.

findings.summary: The CIDR section lists network and host bit counts as loose fragments, so a learner cannot tell which label goes with which value.
findings.evidence:
10.1.4.0/22
address/prefix
22 network bits
first 22 bits
10 host bits
32 - 22
findings.fix: Present it as a small table or annotated diagram of the 32 bits: 22 network bits | 10 host bits, with /22 pointing at the split.

findings.summary: The classful table gives no way to see why 127 is excluded from the Class A range beyond a trailing bullet, and the 'Waste' bullet bundles a number with a historical conclusion.
findings.evidence:
Waste: a /8 gives ~16M hosts even if you need 300
That waste is why CIDR replaced classful addressing
findings.fix: Keep these as two separate bullets, and note in the table that Class A is 1-126 because 127 is loopback.

findings.summary: The block size and worked example is written as bare labels and values with no visual showing where 192.168.1.130 lands among the /26 blocks.
findings.fix: Add a small number-line or table of the four blocks (.0-.63, .64-.127, .128-.191, .192-.255) and mark the block holding .130.

findings.summary: VLSM is listed as four labels with no worked example showing why largest-first keeps blocks aligned and non-overlapping.
findings.evidence: "Sort | largest need first", "Place | aligned boundary", "Next | previous broadcast + 1", "Repeat | smaller blocks"
findings.fix: Add a short example, e.g. allocate 100, 50 and 10 hosts from 192.168.1.0/24 as /25, /26 and /28, listing each network and broadcast address.

findings.summary: The summarization alignment rule is asserted but never explained, so a learner cannot test other pairs of blocks.
findings.evidence: "192.168.1.0/24 + 192.168.2.0/24 are adjacent but cannot form a /23."
findings.fix: State that a /23 block starts on an even third octet (0, 2, 4 ...). 192.168.1.0 is not on that boundary, while 192.168.0.0 is.

findings.summary: The VLSM procedure is a four-step process with no worked example, so the steps are abstract.
findings.evidence:
Sort
largest need first
Place
aligned boundary
Next
previous broadcast + 1
Repeat
smaller blocks
findings.fix: Add a short worked example, e.g. 100, 50 and 10 hosts allocated in order with resulting networks, or a diagram of blocks laid out in the address space.

findings.summary: The 'Not aligned' example states the conclusion without showing why the two adjacent /24s fail to form a /23.
findings.evidence: 192.168.1.0/24 + 192.168.2.0/24 are adjacent but cannot form a /23.
findings.fix: Add the reason: a /23 must start on an even third octet, so 192.168.1.0/23 would not be a valid network boundary.

findings.summary: The NAT flow is a list of fragments rather than an ordered sequence, so the translation steps are hard to follow.
findings.evidence:
Host 10.0.0.5
private source
NAT router
rewrites source IP
Translation table
remembers mapping
Reply
mapped back to host
findings.fix: Draw it as a left-to-right flow diagram: Host 10.0.0.5 -> NAT router (rewrite source, record in table) -> Internet -> reply -> table lookup -> Host.

findings.summary: The link-local row lists the cause in the Span column and uses 'Kind' inconsistently with the other rows, and 127.0.0.0/8 is grouped with RFC 1918 ranges under one heading.
findings.evidence:
169.254.0.0/16
APIPA, DHCP failed
link-local
127.0.0.0/8
this host
loopback
findings.fix: Keep the Span column for the address span or meaning, and put the cause (DHCP failed) in a separate note; label the table 'Special Ranges' with a Kind column consistently.

findings.summary: The 'Port is not connection' callout restates the 4-tuple idea already given in section 2 and the term 'socket' is defined as IP+port while a TCP connection is a 4-tuple, which blurs whether a 'socket' is an endpoint or a connection.
findings.evidence: Socket = IP address + port / A port names a process. Only the 4-tuple names a TCP connection.
findings.fix: Add one line clarifying that a socket is one endpoint and a connection is a pair of sockets (the 4-tuple).

findings.summary: MSL is used in the TIME_WAIT explanation but never defined.
findings.evidence: "Active closer holds TIME_WAIT for 2×MSL (about 60s)"
findings.fix: Add a line such as "MSL = maximum segment lifetime, the longest a packet can survive in the network", so 2×MSL reads as a derived value.

findings.summary: The teardown bullet packs three ideas (four steps, half-close, independent directions) into one line, and the TIME_WAIT bullet's reason line holds two ideas.
findings.evidence: Four steps: each direction closes independently (half-close) / Why: late packets expire, and the final ACK can be resent
findings.fix: Split into separate bullets: 'Four steps', 'Each direction closes independently (half-close)', 'TIME_WAIT: late packets expire', 'TIME_WAIT: final ACK can be resent'.

findings.summary: RTO is used as if the learner knew it, and the chapter never says what it is.
findings.evidence: "3 duplicate ACKs → retransmit at once, no wait for the RTO"
findings.fix: Expand it on first use: "retransmission timeout, the timer after which an unacked segment is resent".

findings.summary: The ISN section's bullets are fragments that each hold a separate idea, and the second and third mix cause and effect without a clear label.
findings.evidence: Stale packets from an old connection are not accepted as new / Blind spoofing becomes hard to guess
findings.fix: Rewrite as 'ISN random per connection → (1) stale packets from old connections rejected, (2) blind spoofing hard to guess', or use a two-row Benefit table.

findings.summary: Two ideas share the same page section: ISN and fast retransmit sit together under one heading, and the 'Interview Point' block is numbered as section 3 after a 'Remember' callout, so the structure is hard to skim.
findings.evidence: 2. ISN and Fast Retransmit ... 3. Interview Point
findings.fix: Split into 'ISN' and 'Fast Retransmit' sections, and keep the Interview Point block unnumbered like on other pages.

findings.summary: The cwnd bullet is placed before the formula and crams a definition and a cross-reference into one line, so the main rule is introduced after a tangent.
findings.evidence: cwnd = sender's own congestion window, a network-side limit (see congestion control)
findings.fix: State 'In flight ≤ min(rwnd, cwnd)' first, then give rwnd and cwnd one short bullet each (or a two-row table) and drop the 'see congestion control' pointer.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "duplicate", "restarts").
findings.evidence: Timeout drops cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts slow start; 3 duplicate ACKs (Reno) halve cwnd and continue in fast recovery
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: MSS is used as the unit for cwnd and is never defined.
findings.evidence: "Slow start: cwnd ~10 MSS, doubles every RTT until ssthresh"; "cwnd = 1 MSS"
findings.fix: Define MSS (maximum segment size, the largest data payload per segment) on first use. Also define ssthresh and RTT, because the page 5 diagram and bullets use them without introduction.

findings.summary: The cwnd diagram's label shows 'doubling, then +1, then drop' while the bullets use ~10 MSS start and ssthresh is only marked at 41 after the loss, so a learner cannot tell which ssthresh ended slow start (the pre-loss threshold is never given).
findings.evidence: Slow start: cwnd ~10 MSS, doubles every RTT until ssthresh ... 10 20 40 80 81 82 41 ssthresh loss
findings.fix: Give the initial ssthresh value (e.g. 80) in the diagram and label the point where growth switches from doubling to +1.

findings.summary: The Loss Reaction section is written as arrow text lines rather than a table, and the repeated 'Loss signal?' prefix makes the comparison harder to scan.
findings.evidence: Loss signal? --timeout--> cwnd = 1 MSS, slow start
findings.fix: Use a two-row table: Signal | Reaction (timeout → cwnd=1 MSS, slow start; 3 dup ACKs (Reno) → cwnd halves, fast recovery).

findings.summary: The cheat sheet's debug section shows a fix and an error explanation as a loose pair of lines, and the Quick recall block's handshake diagram is only labels with no ordering cue, mixing unrelated recall items.
findings.evidence: 'Address already in use' = port bound or in TIME_WAIT / Servers: set SO_REUSEADDR before bind
findings.fix: Present as a two-column 'Symptom | Fix' row, and separate the handshake diagram from the one-line formulas in Quick recall.

findings.summary: The cold-lookup walk is a process written as stacked text lines, with no diagram showing the sequence of queries and referrals.
findings.evidence: Resolver asks root / referral: .com TLD NS / Resolver asks TLD / referral: example.com NS / Resolver asks authoritative / returns the A record
findings.fix: Draw it as a single flow diagram: stub → resolver → root → TLD → authoritative, with each referral labelled on its arrow.

findings.summary: The glue bullet packs the definition into one line, and the circularity explanation is a fragment without a stated cause.
findings.evidence: Glue = A/AAAA of a nameserver inside the zone it serves / ns1.example.com serves example.com: circular without it
findings.fix: Split it into bullets: (1) problem: the NS name sits inside the zone it serves, so resolving it needs the zone first; (2) fix: the parent returns glue A/AAAA in the referral; (3) example: ns1.example.com for example.com.

findings.summary: The MX code block shows the command and the '10 is tried before 20' note before the idea is stated, and the note is separated from the output it explains.
findings.evidence:
bash
dig example.com MX +short
10 is tried before 20
output
10 mail1.example.com.
20 mail2.example.com.
findings.fix: Put the one-line idea 'lower priority number is tried first' before the code, then show the command with its output and drop the stray note between them.

findings.summary: A bullet holds two ideas, the CNAME exclusivity rule and the apex consequence, and the table repeats this content.
findings.evidence: A CNAME cannot share its name with any other record / So no CNAME at the apex: use ALIAS/ANAME or A
findings.fix: Keep the exclusivity rule as one bullet and the apex workaround as a separate bullet. Do not repeat the rule in the table and the 'Classic mistakes' box.

findings.summary: The macOS flush command shown is incomplete; `dscacheutil -flushcache` alone does not clear the mDNSResponder DNS cache on modern macOS.
findings.evidence: sudo dscacheutil -flushcache / Windows / systemd-resolved / macOS
findings.fix: Use `sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder` for macOS.

findings.summary: The TTL change procedure is shown as a bare sequence of steps with no timing labels, and 'Switch record' sits between the two TTL steps without saying when each happens.
findings.evidence: Lower TTL / one old TTL ahead / Switch record / Raise TTL
findings.fix: Show it as a timeline: T−old TTL lower TTL → T switch record → T+new TTL raise TTL, with the time gaps labelled.

findings.summary: The flush-command block lists three commands without saying which OS each is for until a trailing line, so a learner cannot map them.
findings.evidence: ipconfig /flushdns / resolvectl flush-caches / sudo dscacheutil -flushcache / Windows / systemd-resolved / macOS
findings.fix: Put the OS next to each command, as a table with columns OS and Command.

findings.summary: The table says `dig example.com MX` also returns AAAA, TXT and NS records, but dig queries only the single record type given.
findings.evidence: dig example.com MX | also AAAA, TXT, NS
findings.fix: Reword to 'MX records only; swap the type for AAAA, TXT, NS, etc.'

findings.summary: The nslookup table has its 'set type=MX' and 'nslookup' rows mismatched: the interactive-mode result is attached to the wrong row, and the 'older, less detail than dig' note is mislabeled as a command's result.
findings.evidence: set type=MX / interactive mode / nslookup / older, less detail than dig
findings.fix: Make the rows 'nslookup' → 'interactive mode, then set type=MX', and move 'older, less detail than dig' into a separate note under the table.

findings.summary: The 'Common mistakes' list repeats mistakes from page 3 and mixes unrelated debugging causes in one list, so it reads as a restatement rather than a new idea.
findings.evidence: CNAME at the apex / MX pointing at a CNAME or IP
findings.fix: Link back to page 3 rather than repeating them, or keep only the dig-specific mistakes (trailing dot, testing before TTL expiry, wrong registrar NS).

findings.summary: The cheat sheet's closing line mixes the negative-cache rule with the change workflow, and its debug block has no commands labeled by purpose.
findings.evidence: dig +short example.com / dig @8.8.8.8 example.com / dig +trace example.com / dig -x 203.0.113.5 / nslookup -type=MX example.com 8.8.8.8
findings.fix: Add a short purpose comment to each command, for example '# answer only', '# ask one resolver', '# walk from root', '# reverse lookup'.

findings.summary: The answers to the check-yourself questions are written as bare fragments, so the first answer does not state the cause that the question asks about.
findings.evidence: Resolvers that cached before 10:00 keep the 86400 s copy / The new TTL applies only after they refetch
findings.fix: Open with the cause in one sentence: 'The old 86400 s TTL was already cached, so the 300 s TTL took effect only at the next refetch, up to 24 h later.' Then give the fix.

findings.summary: The request/response message-shape comparison is flattened into a stream of labels with no clear table or diagram structure.

findings.fix: Render it as a two-column table (Request vs Response) with rows Start line, Headers, Blank line, Body, or as a single annotated diagram.

findings.summary: The URL anatomy is a flat list of alternating tokens, so the learner cannot see which part is which.

findings.fix: Show the full URL once as a code line and put the parts in a two-column table (part, example) or an annotated diagram.

findings.summary: The error codes are one run-together list with no grouping or table, and each code carries a different kind of fact (name, cause, culprit).

findings.summary: The ETag revalidation flow is a flat list of labels, so the order of steps is lost.
findings.evidence: ETag / server sends / If-None-Match / client revalidates / 304 / reuse cached copy
findings.fix: Show it as a numbered flow or sequence: server sends ETag, client sends If-None-Match, server replies 304, client reuses the cached copy.

findings.summary: The Max-Age / Expires bullet holds two ideas (lifetime and scope), and the cookie example is shown before the idea behind it.
findings.evidence: Max-Age / Expires: lifetime; Path / Domain: scope
findings.fix: Split lifetime and scope into separate bullets and put a one-line explanation of Set-Cookie and Cookie before the http block.

findings.summary: The 'Negotiation' section is a flat list of fragments, so the sequence is not clear.
findings.evidence: TLS handshake / ALPN picks h2 / Response / Alt-Svc: h3 / QUIC connection / HTTP/3 next
findings.fix: Write it as a numbered flow: (1) ALPN in the TLS handshake picks h2; (2) the response advertises Alt-Svc: h3; (3) the client opens a QUIC connection for HTTP/3.

findings.summary: The head-of-line blocking row mixes a scope (per connection) and a level (TCP level), and its meaning is unclear to a skimmer.
findings.evidence: HOL blocking | per connection | TCP level | own stream only
findings.fix: Use consistent wording, e.g. 'one request blocks the rest' / 'a lost TCP packet stalls all streams' / 'a lost packet stalls only its own stream'.

findings.summary: The 'Takes 1 round trip' bullet group mixes several ideas (the key exchange, the cipher, forward secrecy) in a way that reads as a list of loose facts, and the handshake diagram is a flat label sequence.
findings.evidence: ClientHello / versions, ciphers, key share / ServerHello / + certificate + key share / Derive keys / both sides / Finished / data flows
findings.fix: Present the handshake as a numbered client/server sequence and keep one bullet each for key exchange, bulk cipher and forward secrecy.

findings.summary: Page 6 'Cookie flags to always set' leaves the cookie flags unexplained.
findings.evidence: Cookie flags to always set: HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
findings.fix: Add a short gloss per flag, for example a one-line table of the flag and its effect.

findings.summary: Several bullets on the cheat sheet hold more than one idea, and the last bullet strings four failure modes together.
findings.evidence: s_client shows the cert chain; failures: expired cert, hostname mismatch, missing intermediate, untrusted CA
findings.fix: Split into one bullet for what s_client shows and a separate list of the four failure causes.

gaps: Data link layer details: Ethernet, MAC addresses, ARP, VLANs
Routing fundamentals: static routes, OSPF, BGP, default gateway
DHCP and how hosts get addresses
overlaps: Port numbers and the TCP/UDP transport protocols are touched on in osi-tcpip, tcp-udp and dns (DNS over UDP/TCP)
Layer 3 addressing and the IP/NAT concepts appear in both osi-tcpip and ip-subnetting
Encapsulation and the layered protocol stack are reintroduced in tcp-udp and http-tls (HTTP/3 over QUIC/UDP vs TCP)
Each chapter repeats a mental model and cheat sheet that restate the layered picture
